question: What purpose did unit identification markings painted on USAAF aircraft serve during the Second World War?
answer: USAAF unit identification aircraft markings, commonly called "tail markings," were numbers, letters, geometric symbols, and colors painted onto the tails, wings, or fuselages of USAAF aircraft during the Second World War. Their purpose was to serve as call signs in RAF radio procedures used in the UK and to provide a visual means of identification in conjunction with call procedures, and later assembly and combat visual identification of units and aircraft. Two-letter squadron codes denoted a squadron, and an additional single letter, the Radio Call Letter (RCL), identified the aircraft within the squadron. As USSTAF bomber formations grew, assembly necessitated better visual unit identification at greater distance. To facilitate control among thousands of bombers, the USAAF devised a system of aircraft tail markings in 1943 to identify groups and wings.

question: Why was the Greenhouse Item nuclear test of 1951 historically significant in the development of nuclear weapons?
answer: The Greenhouse-Item test, conducted on May 25, 1951, at Engebi Island in the Eniwetok Atoll, was historically significant as the first test of a boosted fission weapon. In this test, deuterium-tritium (D-T) gas was injected into the enriched uranium core of a fission bomb; the heat of the fissioning core produced thermonuclear fusion reactions within the D-T gas (though not enough to constitute a full fusion bomb), and the fusion released free neutrons that greatly increased the efficiency of the fission reaction, yielding 45.5 kilotons—about twice the yield of the unboosted bomb. The device, code-named "Booster" (a name coined by Edward Teller in September 1947), was primarily a research experiment to test nuclear principles and gather data rather than a weaponizable design; as of 1954 no boosted weapon had entered the U.S. nuclear stockpile, and the test's value lay in its research results.
